evals.name: explain-two-confusable-metrics
evals.prompt: I keep mixing up Contextual Precision and Contextual Recall. Explain the difference to me in plain english - what does each one actually compare against what. Write it to explain-contextual.md
evals.expected_output: A markdown file opening on a concrete worked example with real chunk/score values, defining jargon at point of use, a contrast table, one everyday analogy after the mechanism, and a one-line closing. Short paragraphs, bullets over prose.
assertions: Opens on a concrete worked example with real values (a trace, numbers, named fields) rather than an abstract definition
No prose paragraph exceeds 3 sentences
Uses a table or bullet list for the central contrast rather than parallel paragraphs
Structural lines (bullets/table rows) are at least 25% of the body — bullets favoured over prose
Contains exactly one everyday analogy, and it appears after the mechanism is explained, not instead of it
Defines each jargon term inline at first use rather than in a glossary up front
Closing takeaway is a single sentence
No hedging ('may sometimes', 'generally advisable', 'several aspects to consider') and no preamble ('let's break this down')
Correctly states what each metric compares: Contextual Precision is about the ORDER/ranking of retrieved chunks, Contextual Recall is about COVERAGE of the expected output
Makes clear both metrics need expected_output, i.e. they are reference-based

evals.name: explain-why-answer-is-weak
evals.prompt: In an eval interview, a candidate is asked 'Your judge scores 0.9 and the customer says the output is terrible. Who is wrong?' and answers: 'The judge is a strong model so I'd trust the score, and I'd ask the customer for specific examples.' Explain in plain english why that reads as a weak answer. Save it to why-weak.md
evals.expected_output: Concedes the correct part of the intuition first, then a concrete run showing the mechanism, what the judge is actually looking at, one analogy, and a one-line payoff. Bullets and one-liners, not essay prose.
assertions: Opens on a concrete worked example with real values (a trace, numbers, named fields) rather than an abstract definition
No prose paragraph exceeds 3 sentences
Uses a table or bullet list for the central contrast rather than parallel paragraphs
Structural lines (bullets/table rows) are at least 25% of the body — bullets favoured over prose
Contains exactly one everyday analogy, and it appears after the mechanism is explained, not instead of it
Defines each jargon term inline at first use rather than in a glossary up front
Closing takeaway is a single sentence
No hedging ('may sometimes', 'generally advisable', 'several aspects to consider') and no preamble ('let's break this down')
Concedes the correct part of the candidate's intuition before criticising it
Names the actual failure: the judge was never validated against human judgement — agreement was never measured, so a uniformly generous judge passes untouched
